name: Babassu oil

lead: Babassu oil is a pale yellow vegetable oil pressed from the kernels of the babassu palm of northeastern Brazil. It is chemically close to coconut oil, rich in lauric acid, and melts near skin temperature, which is why it is described as spreading easily and feeling less greasy than many oils.

In cosmetics it is used as an emollient in conditioners, hair masks, soaps and lotions. People reach for it to soften hair, tame frizz and add shine, or to moisturise skin, often as a coconut-oil alternative with less scent. Brand and retailer descriptions emphasise these benefits; published laboratory work has focused on its composition and on other applications.

paras: Users apply it to the hair lengths as a pre-wash treatment, leave-in or warm deep-conditioning mask, or use it on skin as a light body oil. It also appears as an ingredient in soaps, balms and shampoo products, and it is sold as a refined, virgin or organic-grade oil.

As a plant oil used topically it is generally treated as a low-risk cosmetic ingredient, though any plant oil can irritate or cause allergy in some people, and heavy application may weigh down fine hair according to user reviews. Like coconut oil it is mostly saturated fat, which reviewers flag when discussing dietary use.

angle.text: Babassu oil is applied as a conditioning oil or mask to soften hair, reduce the look of frizz and add shine, and as a light moisturiser on skin. It is often chosen by people who like coconut oil's feel but want a different scent or weight.

lead: Babassu oil is a pale yellow oil extracted from the kernels of the babassu palm (Attalea speciosa), which grows in the Amazon basin and especially in Maranhao state in northeastern Brazil.[1][2] It is dominated by saturated fatty acids with lauric acid at roughly half of its content, giving it a profile similar to coconut oil.[1]

In hair and skin care it is used as a conditioning and moisturising oil: it melts at about body temperature and is described by suppliers as absorbing without a heavy residue.[1] People use it to add softness, shine and manageability to hair and as a lightly scented alternative to coconut oil. Much of the product's positioning comes from brands and retailers rather than controlled studies.

Scientific literature on babassu covers its fatty-acid and triacylglycerol composition, its by-products (such as mesocarp flour) and their phytochemicals, animal feed and animal feed and industrial uses; it does not include human trials on hair or skin outcomes.[3][4][5]
infobox: Refined, virgin or extra-virgin oil; ingredient in soaps and conditioners

paras: The babassu palm is native to the Amazon region and dominates the babacu forests of Maranhao and Piaui; it is harvested mostly from wild stands rather than plantations.[2][1] Kernels are separated from the hard shell by hand or machine and the oil is obtained by pressing or solvent extraction. Cold-pressed oil is preferred for cosmetic and edible grades.[1]

Brazilian production is concentrated among rural households, including women known as quebradeiras de coco (coconut breakers), who crack the nuts by hand.[1] The residue after pressing is a high-protein cake used mainly as animal feed; the palm also supplies charcoal, flour, thatch and other products.[2]

Babassu oil is mostly saturated: lauric acid (about 50%) and myristic acid predominate, with smaller amounts of oleic and linoleic acid and a low iodine value.[1] A physicochemical study compared extra-virgin and virgin babassu oils produced by different extraction methods, characterising their lipid profiles and thermal behaviour.[3]

A 2024 review of babassu by-products describes free fatty acids, polyphenols, phytosterols and triterpenes in the fruit and discusses laboratory findings on antioxidant, antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity of those compounds.[5]

sections.h: Use in hair and skin care
paras: Cosmetic suppliers describe babassu oil as an emollient that helps hair hold moisture, aids detangling, and makes hair easier to comb, and some say it forms a light barrier against heat styling. These descriptions come from sellers and blogs and have not been tested in published controlled trials. Reviewers on retail sites note that it can feel heavy on thin or fine hair unless used as a short warm treatment.
On skin it is used as a light body oil and as an ingredient in soaps, balms and lotions, often in place of coconut or palm-derived oils.[1]

No studies found. Related laboratory and animal work includes a microemulsion of babassu oil tested on immune cells in vitro, and feeding trials in lambs and dairy cows using babassu oil or bran.[4][6][7]

Babassu oil is high in saturated fat, which reviewers note when discussing dietary use alongside other lauric oils.[1] Topical plant oils can occasionally cause irritation or allergy in individual users.
